newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk leftists, generals take aim at Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Turk leftists, generals take aim at Islamists.

text.p: Leftist MPs and the influential armed forces, alarmed by the ruling Islamists' radicalism, have ganged up on Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan in a show of secularist sabre-rattling.

The Democratic Left Party and the rival Republican People's Party each announced on Wednesday the filing of censure motions against Erbakan's coalition with foreign minister pro-Western Tansu Ciller to safeguard the country's secular system.
However, prospects for unseating the government remained uncertain at best when the matter comes to a vote, within 16 to 23 days.
The two factions control just 122 seats in the 550-member parliament, with the main opposition Motherland Party so far reluctant to support the measure on tactical grounds.

Ciller, meanwhile, survived another scare when deputies voted 269 to 259 against setting up a formal inquiry into allegations she was involved in corruption at the state-owned Turban hotel and tourism company.
The decision was a replay of an earlier vote last month, marred by charges of voting irregularities, and could have sent her to the Supreme Court for investigation and trial.

The political drama came as Turkey's generals stepped up their war of nerves with the government, using an anti-Islamist newspaper to caution it was straying too far from the secular path staked out by Kemal Ataturk, creator of the modern state.
"The values of our country are being trampled underfoot," the leftist daily Cumhuriyet on Wednesday quoted senior force commanders as saying at a meeting earlier in the week.
The officers also complained that existing Turkish institutions -- an apparent reference to parliament and the courts -- had failed to step in and protect the secular state.

On Tuesday, the army diverted an armoured column on training manoeuvres through an Islamist stronghold -- a tactic lost on no one in a country that has seen three interventions by the armed forces in the last 37 years.

Daily newspapers and independent television all featured pictures of tanks and armoured personnel carriers in the streets of the Ankara district of Sincan, where pro-Islamists had earlier demonstrated for an end to secular rule.
"Sincan Manoeuvres Shake the Government," said the daily Milliyet, in a typical headline.

Police on Wednesday arrested the mayor of Sincan, Bekir Yildiz, for hosting the event. State-run Anatolian news agency said he was taken to Ankara security court for questioning on charges of anti-secular activities.

At issue are proposals during the Moslem holy month of Ramadan to reassert the Moslem credentials of Erbakan and his Welfare Party: lifting the ban on Islamic headscarves for women civil servants and paving the road for overland pilgrimages to the Moslem holy city of Mecca.
Other measures include construction of mosques in historic secularist strongholds, including the Christian quarter of the former Ottoman capital.
"It is seen that the incidents in Sincan are trying the patience of the soldiers and the need was felt for a warning," columnist Bilal Cetin wrote in the liberal Yeni Yuzyil.
"What are we going to do? Are we going to wait for tanks to go another 20 km into the streets of Ankara?" he asked.
It was not clear, however, that the divided opposition was capable of bringing down the government when the measures come to a vote -- between 16 and 23 days from the date of filing.

Passage of a censure motion, essentially a vote of no confidence, requires an absolute majority of parliament. To date, the coalition controls a narrow margin in the 550-seat body although there may be some defections.
The main opposition Motherland Party has hinted such a challenge is premature, preferring to wait for the government to collapse under its own weight.
"We handed it (the censure proposal) to the speaker of parliament at 11 o'clock last night," a spokesman for the Democratic Left Party told Reuters.
"Turkey's democratic and secular republic is being exposed to a serious threat and dangerous environment in the hands of this regime," the DSP said in an accompanying statement.
The statement said the ruling Welfare Party was "closing its eyes to violations of the constitutional state".
